--- title: '1D diffusion model solution' author: 'Sasha D. Hafner' format: gfm: default --- Let's start by looking at the measurement data. We'll use pandas. ::: {.cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd ``` ::: ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} measdat = pd.read_csv('col_salt.csv') measdat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Seems we have even 1 d spacing in time, which is convenient. We can match that exactly without changing the `diff1D()` function and align model output and measurements without a merge operation. Load our model function. ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import diff_mod as dm ``` ::: And other modules. ::: {.cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ``` ::: So here is our model call. ::: {.cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} pred01 = dm.diff1D( L = 0.1, n = 50, D = 1.6E-9, bc = [36, 0], ci = 0, t_eval = np.linspace(0, 20 * 86400, 21) ) ``` ::: And we can use the same approach that was shown in the exercise for calculating accumulation. We will need the cross-sectional area. ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} area = np.pi * (0.02 / 2)**2 area ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0.0003141592653589793 ``` ::: ::: The `numpy.sum()` function accepts an axis parameter (second parameter). The help file doesn't really illuminate how to set it, but with experimentation you can figure out how to add up all the columns, so you have one sum per time. ::: {.cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} salt_mod = (pred01['c'] * pred01['dx'] * area).sum(0) salt_mod ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` array([0. , 0.00014977, 0.000212 , 0.00025964, 0.00029939, 0.00033354, 0.00036318, 0.00038899, 0.0004115 , 0.00043113, 0.00044826, 0.00046321, 0.00047625, 0.00048763, 0.00049756, 0.00050622, 0.00051377, 0.00052037, 0.00052612, 0.00053114, 0.00053552]) ``` ::: ::: We should check to make sure that this output array has the same length as the number of times. It does: 21. Units here are kg, and the measurement data are in mg. And time there is in h. If we are sure that we used the right times in the model call, we could just add a column with model output. We'll start with that. First, make a new data frame that will hold measurements and model output. ::: {.cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} mmdat = measdat.copy() ``` ::: And add the model output we processed above. ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} mmdat['salt_mod_mg'] = salt_mod * 1E6 mmdat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

This would work even if we had some times in the model output that were not present in the measurement DataFrame, or vice versa. For that we need to combine model time and our response variable. And it is easiest to merge in a DataFrame, so we'll do that. ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} moddat = pd.DataFrame({ 'time_d': pred01['t'] / 86400, 'salt_mod_mg': salt_mod * 1E6 }) moddat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Finally, let's plot the results for comparison. ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} plt.plot(mmdat2.time_d, mmdat2.salt_mg, marker = 'o', label = 'Measured') plt.plot(mmdat2.time_d, mmdat2.salt_mod_mg, marker = 'o', label = 'Model output') plt.xlabel('Time (d)') plt.ylabel('Column NaCl (mg)') plt.legend() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](validation_solution_files/figure-commonmark/cell-13-output-1.png){} ::: ::: Well, clearly the model underestimates NaCl accumulation, even if we consider that there is some random error in measurements (see it?). But measurements and the model both show the same shape and are not terribly far off. We can get quantitative using the model fit statistics we discussed in class on Thursday. Let's load the module. ::: {.cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} import mod_fit as mf ``` ::: First mean bias. ::: {.cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} mf.mbe(mmdat.salt_mg, mmdat.salt_mod_mg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` np.float64(-42.657897805438154) ``` ::: ::: So that's a mean bias of under 10% of the maximum. That would not be terrible for an environmental model, but depending on the application, better accuracy might be needed. Mean absolute error is similar. ::: {.cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} mf.mae(mmdat.salt_mg, mmdat.salt_mod_mg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` np.float64(42.657897805438154) ``` ::: ::: Not surprising, from looking at the plot, which shows that most of the error is related to bias.
